findings.body: The old code used a `pending` map so that N concurrent `loadCached(key, fn)` calls would only invoke `fn` once and share the resulting promise. findings.title: Fire-and-forget fetch silently swallows errors and always reports success
findings.body: The function previously awaited the fetch and returned `response.ok`, letting callers know whether the request succeeded. Now it fires the request without awaiting it and unconditionally returns `true`. If the fetch fails (network error, non-2xx response), the caller sees success anyway and the error is invisible — unhandled rejections are suppressed by `void`. The function is still `async` but nothing is awaited; the `async` marker is misleading. Either await the response and return `response.ok` as before, or if a fire-and-forget pattern is truly wanted, remove the `async` and `return true` and instead handle errors (e.g., with `.catch()`) so failures are observable.

findings.title: Swallowed JSON parse and validation errors silently return defaults
findings.body: The catch-all on line 42 swallows every `JSON.parse` failure and returns `{}`, so a settings file with malformed JSON, a missing comma, or an unquoted key is silently ignored. The previous code threw `Invalid settings JSON at ${path}: <parse error>`, which told the user exactly which file was broken and why. Equally, when the parsed value is `null`, a non-object, or an array (lines 38-40), the function returns `{}` instead of throwing `Settings at ${path} must be a JSON object.`. Because `loadSettings` merges the result with `DEFAULT_SETTINGS`, users get silently working-but-wrong defaults and have no path to discover that their configuration file is corrupt or contains a typo. Restore the previous error-throwing behavior, or at minimum log the error to stderr or a configured logger so the failure is visible.
